en: a wise person should first apply the state of being the second letter to the first letter that is followed by a sibilant (ūṣman), whether it stands at the beginning or in the middle of a word. 1.
If there is no doubling of the first letter of a word— provided that a primary initial [consonant] follows it— this applies except for the sibilants and aspirates (ś,
ṣ, s, h). Furthermore, doubling never occurs for the letter *r* or for the letter *h*.
And never [should there be doubling] of the second letter of a class, nor of a fourth;
that which is preceded by a consonant is called "doubling," whereas doubling preceded by a vowel shall never occur.
In the *Kāṭhaka*, however, "filling the gap" (*pṛṇacchidram*) is designated as "duality" (*dvitvam*); thus, once [the word] has departed, "filling the gap" as duality would never exist.
Furthermore, let there be a subsequent *laṣ* for the sake of the heap; even when unjoined, it does not reach duality.
Wherever the conjunction of consonants is prohibited by a specific rule,
there a doubling occurs by that very rule; for indeed, the doubling of the letter *la* occurs with the letter *va* only when it follows a vowel.
In that way it would be conjoined, and likewise un-conjoined, and otherwise.
(7) Wherever a *n* preceded by *r* is seen at the end of a word, one should recognize a specific rule there; this is called "doubling" (*dvitva*). (8)
It is proclaimed that a vowel following the letter *ra* functions as a consonant;
therefore, the grammatical operations pertaining to conjuncts (*saṃyukta*) indeed take place according to the rule. [This occurs] when a *ra* following a long vowel stands before the vowel *ṛ*.
The *repha* (the letter *r*) shall be a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the preceding vowel, and this shall likewise apply even after a short vowel.

Furthermore, that *bhakti* (the transitional sound) which arises at the end of a word following a long vowel is also a constituent part of the preceding vowel; otherwise, it would result in a fault. (10–11)
Thus ends the definition of duality.
